items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I’m still trying to figure out this team a little bit’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Is Mike Brown still coaching the Knicks? How’s that possible!?

Should Leon Rose trade everybody and quit on the spot? Would it be better for New York to tank the season?

Dumb questions without legitimate answers!

On the Knicks’ slow start and still figuring out the team’s identity:

“I haven’t even looked at 50 wins, or 45 or 52 or anything like that. I’m still trying to figure out this team a little bit. I know everybody is like, ‘Whoa, it’s the same team as last year. New season, new team, new challenges, and so I’m not even sure who I wanna play yet, you know? Trying to figure the little things out.”

On Mikal Bridges’ shooting struggles against the Celtics:

“Mikal had three or four wide-open 3s. And obviously we want him to make half of them if they’re open. But he’s got to keep shooting. And hopefully they’ll eventually go in — sooner than later. But he’s getting the looks that he needs to get. He just has to knock them down now. And he’s got to make sure he’s physical on the defensive end.”

On Bridges and the Knicks needing to play more physically on defense:

“He’s got to make sure that he’s physical on the defensive end. And he, as well as everybody else because it was all of us, are laying on screens when we get hit, and that when we do switch, there’s a level of physicality to the switch so that they’re not able to take advantage of us.”

On what went wrong for the Knicks in the 107-103 loss to Boston:

“It was a physical ball game, and we have to give Boston credit. They had the advantage with the physicality.”

On Jayson Tatum’s 36-point performance against the Knicks:

“Jayson Tatum did what Jayson Tatum does. You just take your hat off and say, ‘Good D, better O.’ But that’s not why we lost the game. We lost the game because we didn’t handle their physicality on both ends of the floor for too many stretches that were too long.”

On the Knicks’ progress despite starting the season with two losses:

“I think we took a stride, just not big enough strides. There’s positives and negatives to take from this game. We know what we have to do, and the things I think are glaring to us are controllable. So that’s a positive we can take from this.”

On how the Celtics helped shape the Knicks into a championship team:

“The way they were playing, and I guess how they’re still playing, kind of helped shape our team. They were obviously a dynamic force. And obviously the past couple years with injuries and personnel changes and stuff like that, things are different. We were trying to figure out how we can beat those guys.”

On Mitchell Robinson not watching the Knicks’ championship ring ceremony:

“We know Mitch is a competitor. He’s a person who wears his emotions on his sleeve … that’s just Mitch being Mitch.”

On Robinson leaving the Knicks for the Celtics:

“It’s definitely bittersweet. He’s a good friend. I’m just happy he was able to get a nice payday.”

On having limited involvement in The Roommates Show’s Polymarket sponsorship agreement:

“To be honest, we really don’t have much of a say in terms of a lot of the sales and who they reach out to. I don’t wanna say we know nothing, but we don’t know much about all that stuff.

“I know they sit there and talk about, it’s trading; it’s not gambling.”

On being surprised by the controversy surrounding the Polymarket sponsorship:

“Last year, we had BetMGM. I don’t really know too much around the controversy of it or whatever. I saw some things on Twitter, and I was just like, ‘Oh, I didn’t know people felt that way.’

“I saw a little bit of it the last couple days, and I was shocked — and it might be a little ignorance on my part because I don’t know, but yeah.”

On taking advantage of sponsorship deals to pay the pod employees more:

“When it’s the pod and that, I kind of play ball a little bit because there’s other people depending on that. So it gets brought to us at the very end and for me personally, I’m just like other people are depending on this. So I play ball with that.”

On the Knicks’ locker room without him:

“I know it ain’t no fun no more. I know. I just brought so much light to this team.”

On feeling unwanted by the Knicks during free agency:

“They didn’t want me? Yeah. That’s what it felt like. I was like, cool. There wasn’t bad blood behind it. Man, fresh start.”

On signing with the Celtics despite their rivalry with the Knicks:

“The only thing that was kind of different was going to the rivals. But you know me, man. I like to troll. Nobody was happy with that move. But I was.”

On learning to treat the NBA as a business after years of trade rumors:

“Anything can happen, I can be traded at any moment. I was in so many of those trade talks. I’m like, ‘I just got to see it as a business. You can’t let your feelings in it.’ That’s kind of what I did.”

On his understanding of the NBA’s second-apron salary cap restrictions amid his Knicks exit:

“Not too much. But it is what it is.”

On having a more active offensive role with the Celtics:

“I’m a lot more active. Constantly moving on the offensive end. It’s actually going pretty great. I got to bring the energy.”

On using a championship-ring bait in an employee phishing simulation:

“The company had previously sent out an email to its corporate team as a simulation of a phishing attack designed to strengthen our security against hackers. MSG was recently hacked and extorted using an employee login and password obtained through a similar phishing attack. Using the rings as a lure to gain employees attention was an unfortunate mistake.”

On the narrative about the Knicks’ wrongdoing:

“There is a great deal of misinformation regarding the championship rings. The plan has always been to distribute more than 275 rings and jewelry to the people in the organization who were part of last season’s success. As is common with many teams, the players were always supposed to get their rings as part of the opening night ceremony and then everyone else will receive theirs in about 4-6 weeks. Regarding the phishing email, the process of securing and reminding our employees to protect our IP was not a mistake but the choice to use the ring to do so was a mistake and we apologize to our employees and the fans.

“Winning the championship was a great moment for all New Yorkers. Those who choose to focus on the negative are missing the joy that comes with the team’s accomplishment.”

items.title: Celtics 107, Knicks 103: “I took the over at 58. Still alive.”
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
The Knicks (0-2) traveled to Boston to face the Celtics (1-1) at TD Garden tonight. Each team was fighting for their first win of the season, and clearly pride was on the line. Through the first half, the game teetered to and fro, but the home team gained momentum in the third quarter. After falling behind by 12 in the fourth, New York fought back to a one-point deficit, but, in what felt like a postseason game, Jayson Tatum went on a heater and carried his team to victory, 107-103.

What else is there to say about Mitchell Robinson (4 PTS, 4 RBS, 22 MIN) in a green jersey? It’s a bummer. We keep it moving. Mitch had a lackluster first outing with his new team and started mediocre tonight, too. He managed to put back his own miss over OG Anunoby (20 PTS, 10 RBS, 8 AST), but two fouls sat him after three minutes.

Tatum (36 PTS, 9 RBS, 7 AST) and Paul George (15 PTS, 7 RBS) got the C’s on the board to start, Karl-Anthony Towns (22 PTS, 10 RBS) and Jalen Brunson (19 PTS, 4 AST, 3 TO) scored, and we were off. Neither team impressed from deep, combining to make two of their first seven attempts, a trend that continued through the half. Unlike opening night, the whistles were fairly quiet, and the game had a better pace. The villains were pests on the glass, out-rebounding our heroes and turning five O-boards into five extra shots.

After trailing early, the guests used the free throw line to climb into the lead, and the score stayed closed from there. The ‘Bockers goosed their lead to five, and Boston clawed their way back. The bench contributed positive minutes yet again. Landry Shamet (8 PTS) checked in early to relieve a foul-carrying, blank-shooting Mikal Bridges. Also off the bench, Miles McBride (20 PTS, 6-of-8 3pt) took the floor around the six-minute mark. When he fired from the corner, TD Garden let loose a loud “Deeeuuuccceee” and were rewarded with a swish.

Late in the quarter, Anunoby was the only starter on the court, playing alongside Jose Alvarado, McBride, Shamet, and Andre Drummond. Twice we saw Alvarado wrestling a Celtic for the ball on the floor. His dogged defense helped to preserve a 27-26 lead a the break.

New York gave up five points to Luka Garza to start the second and Mike Brown needed a timeout before two minutes had passed. He replaced Andre Drummond with Karl-Anthony Towns. New York fell behind by eight before restoring their composure. At 7:30, Brunson returned to the fray and led Towns, Hart, and Jordan Clarkson led a comeback to tie the score, which was undone by buckets by Tatum and Neemiias Queta.

Robinson returned and continued to putter ineffectively for about six minutes. New Knicks reserve center, James Wiseman, made his season debut for New York with two minutes left in the half and promptly collected a loose ball foul. Fortunately, Josh Hart connected on his first triple of the night (after four tries) and followed that with an off-balance hook, but George knocked down a buzzer-beater for a 50-49 lead.

In the first half, the Knicks made just 30% from deep; Boston was a shade better at 35%. The orange-and-blue crew had taken 12 free throws to their opponent’s four, and each team had 21 boards at the break. In fact, the teams were nearly identical up and down the board. Towns topped all scorers with 12 points and eight rebounds, while Tatum had 11 points on 11 shots.

Anunoby was a bricklayer in the season opener (3-of-12 FG, 1-of-9 3PT), but his second dinger tonight, plus a cutting layup, got New York humming out of halftime. Jordan Walsh, Tatum, and Derrick White went on an 8-0 run before Brunson laced one from deep. In this game of runs, though, it seemed only a matter of time before one team hit the gas and began packing on a significant lead.

Weirdly, through two-and-a-half quarters, Queta was the only Celtic to take free throws—and just six at that. Clean defense so far by Gotham’s greatest!

Spoke too soon. Drummond gave Towns a breather at the five-minute mark and collected two infractions. After McBride picked off Queta and converted back-to-back treys, the Knicks trailed 70-69. Queta seemed hell-bent to prove his value as the Celtics’ center, hitting more free throws and a corner three to reach 12 points and pad his team’s lead. Shamet fouled on a screen, Drummond picked up a technical foul, Hart mishandled a Brunson pass, and the third frame ended with the Knicks down, 83-73.

Robinson punched back in to start the final period. He bodied Anunoby, blocked Towns, and slammed an alley-oop. The crowd went —and then the big fella committed foul number five. Back to the bench with eight-and-a-half to go. Many watching the Amazon Prime stream at home felt a shiver of déjà vu.

While the deficit reached 12, Bridges provided no offensive support. He shot 2-of-8 in the season opener and whiffed on all eight shots in Boston. He has yet to attempt a free throw this year. With production like that, we weren’t surprised when his night finished at 8:25. Meanwhile, McBride had netted 5-of-7 from deep for 23 points and counting with seven minutes remaining. That’ll bring up the team’s overall percentage!

KAT led the league with 56 double-doubles last season. With four minutes left, he grabbed his tenth board for his second double-double of the new campaign, flushed a Brunson miss, and brought the hole to three.

Hart was a shady shooter from downtown, missing five and making two—but that second one was clutch. Then KAT picked Queta’s pocket and Brunson pulled-up to make the score 99-98.

This might have been game two of the season, but it felt like Game 2 of the ECF. Tatum scored on back-to-back jumpers. OG made two freebies. The deficit was three when Tatum— who was on a heater—connected from deep with 30 seconds left. McBride hit his sixth triple at 14 seconds, but the Knicks were forced to foul and pray. Pritchard made one and missed one, and in the resulting fracas, George fouled Brunson. Cap missed a free throw with four seconds left, intentionally bricked the second, and OG missed a futile, final heave. Ballgame.

Quoth Good names all taken, “I took the over at 58. Still alive.” The season is young, the sky is not falling. After a short offseason and the usual rust, the Knicks have lost two close contests against playoff teams. Our heroes head home to host the O’Magic on Sunday, which should have a more favorable outcome. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.

items.title: Knicks make Dalton Knecht decision involving Kevin McCullar Jr.
items.author: Kento Kato
items.content:
With Karl-Anthony Towns and the New York Knicks’ failed attempt at an extension being public, Miles McBride struggling as he enters a contract year, and Josh Hart and Tyler Kolek also not being extended, fans have speculated on potential roster moves.

And the fans got one today—just not the one most people were necessarily expecting.

On Friday morning, ESPN’s Shams Charania that New York had signed former Tennessee Volunteer and Los Angeles Lakers guard Dalton Knecht to a two-way NBA contract. To make space for the third-year wing, the Knicks are waiving Kevin McCullar Jr.

The Knicks weren’t the only team interested either. On Thursday night, rumors indicated that both the Timberwolves and Raptors were also looking at Knecht.

The former 17th overall pick averaged 9.8PPG and 2.8RPG while shooting 46.1% from the field and 37.6% from three during his rookie season. For spurts, it looked like he could develop into a solid rotation piece for a Lakers team that was still trying to contend with LeBron James at the helm and became a fan favorite after a in the NBA Cup.

Midway through the season, though, Knecht was involved in a trade that would have sent him to the Hornets in exchange for center Mark Williams. After Williams failed his physical and the trade was rescinded, Knecht was forced to return to the Lakers.

Knecht, contrary to belief, finished out the season on a solid note, averaging 8.5PPG while shooting 40.8% from three. Things did take a turn for the worse last season, though. After appearing in 78 games and averaging 19.2MPG in his first season, he averaged just 10.2MPG in just 54 games during the 2025-26 campaign. As many young players do, he struggled with the decreased minutes and inconsistent playing time, leading to a cycle of worse play and even fewer minutes.

The third-year man can still impact the Knicks. He’s just 25 years old and is an above-average shooter with size. In his final year in college, he averaged 21.7PPG on 45.8% shooting from the field and 39.7% shooting from three. It’s not every day you can find that kind of shooting at his height on the waiver wire. But there are plenty of reasons why he saw his minutes dwindle and why he eventually was waived.

Despite being 6’6”, Knecht isn’t much of a defender. He can get lost defensively, and even if he manages to be in the right spots at the right times, he just does not possess the athleticism to be much of a factor on that end. Offensively, he’s shown flashes of being able to utilize his shot to get to other spots on the floor. When a part of the rotation, he was making nice reads off the ball and routinely had nice timely cuts to get easy looks at the rim. But at the end of the day, he’s still best utilized as a spot-up shooter and only a spot-up shooter. He can’t create for himself due to a lack of a reliable handle and certainly doesn’t create for others.

There are also of Knecht not knowing the team’s plays and schemes, which would surely frustrate Mike Brown, who is a very detail- and execution-oriented coach.

Knecht is just 25 years old and has room to grow. If the Knicks, their coaches, and their culture get him right, the shooting and size likely give him more upside than McCullar. But don’t expect him to be a significant contributor. New York likely signed him as a project piece and a deep depth piece. It would take a whole lot for Knecht to not only enter the rotation but to stay there. And in such a circumstance, the Knicks would likely have a lot more than Knecht’s play to worry about.

That being said, it’s still an intriguing low-risk move for a player who may just have needed a change of scenery. It is unfortunate, though, to see McCullar gone given the memorable moments he’s had with this club, regardless of how infrequent they may have been.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘You’re a freaking perennial All-Star, so just make the bucket’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
The schedule won’t give the Knicks a break as New York visits the Celtics on Friday to fight old pal Mitch Robinson in Beantown.

New York’s off to a losing start to their title-defense season, and going against the also-winless Leprechauns won’t make things easier.

Here’s the latest from your beloved Knickerbockers.

On Andre Drummond’s performance in the Knicks’ season opener against the 76ers:

“I thought he played with a lot of bounce, energy, in the first half on both ends of the floor. We probably ran him too long because it looked like in the second half, not just him but especially our five starters, it looked like he ran out of a little bit of gas. I gotta keep getting to know him to see where the minutes may lie for him to be effective. But I thought he was really, really, really good in the first half.”

On Mitchell Robinson signing with the Celtics and facing him on Friday:

“You’re excited for anybody that’s able to help their situation or family, in life, and Boston gave him a nice deal. And so, you want nothing but the best for him because you know him, and he’s a great, great, great dude. But you wanna beat him at the end of the day.

“So it’s gonna be exciting to see him because of the type of person he is and what we all went through together last year. But at the end of the day, we want to kick his [butt] like he probably wants to kick ours.”

On whether the Knicks might use the Hack-a-Mitch strategy against Mitchell Robinson:

“Me personally, I’ve always leaned more to do that come playoff time or later in the season where you’re really trying to gameplan and get certain games. Right now, I want to see if we can defend these guys with what our foundation is.

“If at some point throughout the course of the game it happens, it happens, but right now I’m just trying to think about communice, be physical without foul, no blow-bys, contest and finish every shot, ball pressure—trying to establish a foundation.”

On Karl-Anthony Towns needing to stop drawing unnecessary fouls:

“Some guys, I say, ‘go try to get fouled,’ Nah nah nah. KAT: You’re a freaking perennial All-Star. So just make the bucket, and if he happens to foul you, then great. When you do those types of [foul-baiting] things, it shortens your opportunities to pick up a foul when you’re boxing out or trying to get a rebound and stuff like that, so that’s the stuff we want to try to eliminate from his game.”

On Towns’ improvement with fouls last season:

“To his credit, he got better as [last] year went along. This is a new year, new team, new challenges.”

On allowing Towns to make mistakes while adjusting to the new season:

“I don’t want him to take 10 steps backwards, but if he takes a couple steps backwards and he’s gotta figure it out, I’m OK with it.”

“There was a three that he shot with Maxey closing out to him. He stuck his leg out. He’s a good enough player to where he doesn’t need to look for and/or try to draw the foul. Just make the basket.”

On staying in the locker room during the Knicks’ championship ceremony:

“I feel like I gotta earn it. I don’t want to experience something that I wasn’t there for.

“I want to be able to experience that [celebration] because I was a part of it. I let those guys have their moment.”

On hearing Knicks fans chant his name at Madison Square Garden:

“It was pretty surreal. Just the energy of the arena, just because of how hard I was working, how hard I was playing, just to hear it, I can’t even really explain it. I got chills. Something you live for as a player, hearing the fans be behind you.

“This arena’s electric. Just doing hard work and aggressive plays gets the crowd going, so it gets me going too.”

On learning Mike Brown’s system and adjusting to his coaching style:

“I think it’s been fun for both of us because, obviously, yes, he’s still trying to get to know me and vice versa, I’m trying to get to know him as a coach. I think we surprise each other on a daily basis on the different things that I’m capable of doing as a player. And obviously, the way his coaching style is too, the freedom I have too, is a little bit different. It’s like a tug-and-pull every time we step on the floor with each other. … It’s cool to have the freedom to play the way I want to play, be able to use my experience and my veteran leadership to play the way I want to play but also play the way he wants me to.”

On feeling welcomed by his new Knicks teammates:

“This is a great team. Great core group. They’ve done a great job of incorporating me into the group and making me feel like I’m one of them.”

On being prepared to step in when Karl-Anthony Towns gets into foul trouble:

“I’m always ready when the moment comes. Obviously, we want KAT to play but whenever my number’s called, I always try to be prepared to go.”

On the Knicks’ 0-1 start and the importance of learning from mistakes:

“It’s Game 1. It means literally nothing. We don’t want to be the best version of ourselves game one – if we are, it’s going to be a long season. A lot of mistakes that we have to learn from.”

On the emotional significance of the Knicks’ championship celebration:

“Something like that, it has a special place in your heart. Now, we’re happy that all of that’s over with and we can fully turn the page and focus on this year.”

On receiving his championship ring in front of Knicks fans at Madison Square Garden:

“It was super dope. A moment you dream of.”

On how the Knicks’ locker room has changed since Mitchell Robinson’s departure:

“It’s definitely different. Obviously that’s someone who’s had a big presence here, big presence in the locker room…No one else listens to country [music] but me, so that’s tough in the weight room. The lack of his presence is obviously felt a little bit. That’s why it’s a new team.”

On the Celtics potentially assigning Robinson to guard him:

“They cross match a lot, so I’m sure he’ll be guarding me, so can’t wait to shoot in that… When I make a couple, I’m gonna let him know.”

On what he expects from the Knicks going against Mitch:

“It’s gonna be the same thing. We’re still gonna be battling for rebounds.”

On facing former Knicks teammate Mitchell Robinson and the Celtics:

“It’s bittersweet. You love Mitch — we’ve done so many historical things together here.

“To not see him in a Knicks jersey anymore…we’re a family unit. To not be able to have him with us on this journey after that amazing journey we went through is bittersweet.

“But it’s going to be amazing to be able to see our brother, hug him, show him some love and compete playing basketball like we love to do. We made each other better. He brought the best out of me, and I feel that I was able to bring the best out of him.

“Mitch was a big part of this team winning a championship and probably has the most important offensive rebound in Knicks history.”

On needing to avoid foul trouble and remain available for his teammates:

“All jokes have some truth to it, right? I never want to put my team in that kind of position — I have to do a better job, not only in the regular season but in the postseason, to make sure I’m available for my team.”

On facing the Knicks for the first time since signing with the Celtics:

“It doesn’t matter that I’m playing my former team. It’s more so just trying to bounce back from what happened two days ago. It’s basketball, it’s a business. Got to play the team just like you play any other team.”

On not watching the Knicks’ championship ring ceremony:

“I didn’t watch it. I mean, I was still stuck in my head (about the opening-day loss)… I’m proud of those guys. Obviously I was a part of it. Didn’t really want to watch it.”

On defending Jalen Brunson and approaching his former teammates like any other opponent:

“Just here to play basketball. Same thing I’ll do with any other team, same thing I’ll do with them. It’s just all about basketball.”

On using the Celtics’ season-opening loss as motivation:

“I use it as fuel, kinda have to. Last game we got demolished. As a big, can’t let that happen. I gotta take that on the chin and learn from it, watch the film, and get better, and just focus on the next one.”

On witnessing the Knicks’ championship ceremony after experiencing a similar moment in Cleveland:

“It was a great night for New York fans. Obviously, it’s something… 50+ years. I was a part of that at one point where we hadn’t won a major championship in Cleveland in over 50 years. The fans will never forget this moment, will never forget that championship run.

“We were happy that we were just able to come and play on such a historical night, a historical building, and play the game we love.”

On defending Jalen Brunson and Karl-Anthony Towns:

“Obviously, KAT is very dangerous when he has space. Anytime JB is handling the ball with KAT popping, it creates a long closeout for guys trying to get to that shot.”

items.title: The Knicks finally got their rings, the coaches got boxes
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Imagine your employer had an excellent year and you were in line for an award, one you earned through great effort, extensive travel, and long nights. Instead of receiving it, however, you’re handed an IOU note at the ceremony. Or worse, you were with a fake email about the award, just to test the company’s cybersecurity.

When Vardon describes this very scenario in his latest report, he’s not talking about the slighted workers of a local plumbing supply company. He’s talking about the assistant coaches and staff of the world champion New York Knicks.

At Tuesday’s season opener, the presentation (broadcast nationally on NBC) made it appear the Knicks assistant coaches were receiving championship rings during the pregame banner ceremony. The boxes they were handed? Empty.

It came as no surprise to the assistants. They hadn’t even been fitted for rings, and the empty boxes were a token gesture so they wouldn’t feel left out. Token gestures can backfire on you, though, especially when they seem, perhaps, insincere. The Knicks coaches were upset, according to Vardon, on a scale from mild irritation to very spicy.

In quintessential Knicks fashion, the organization’s statement on the situation is, “We are not disclosing anything about the rings.” Because robots need not acknowledge the petty concerns of disposable humans.

One of the most stunning quotes from Vardon’s piece is this:

“ received conflicting information about whether head coach Mike Brown received his ring on Tuesday and could not immediately verify if he got one.”

What? We can’t confirm if coach Mike Brown got a ring?

The story careens off a cliff from there. Vardon notes, “Many longtime employees at Madison Square Garden, including some who work in the Knicks’ business operations, will not receive rings at all […]. Typically, most employees for NBA teams receive rings, even if they are not as fancy and expensive as the ones the players receive.” Yes, some franchises reward the plebes, but not the NBA’s second-most valuable one. Enter Gordon Gekko, stage left.

However, in September, MSG sent employees a fake championship ring offer. The email congratulated recipients and invited them to select one of two complimentary ring designs: “Championship Gold” or “Garden Classic.” But The email was actually an internal phishing test. Employees who clicked the link were assigned mandatory cybersecurity training rather than receive a ring.

What kind of cold, villainous monster says, “You know how we’re not giving the employees championship rings? One hilarious way to test our cybersecurity would be….”

Oh, the team ain’t hurting for money. The Knicks reportedly generated $640 million in revenue during their championship season, while the franchise’s estimated valuation climbed 29% to $12.6 billion, making it the NBA’s second-most valuable team.

Giving New York the benefit of the doubt, those rings must be difficult to manufacture. Designed by Jason Arasheben of Jason of Beverly Hills, the Knicks’ blingy ring features roughly 800 diamonds and sapphires totaling 22 carats, set in white gold. Its elaborate design includes a mechanical pop-up replica of Madison Square Garden, 16 emerald-cut diamonds representing the team’s playoff victories, and a 0.16-carat diamond set in the Larry O’Brien Trophy. One cannot gaze for long upon the ring before weeping, and it must be returned to Mount Doom post haste!

The Knicks won in mid-June, leaving about four months for design, contract, and construction. That’s a tight schedule. Delays aren’t unprecedented in the NBA, and according to team sources, the assistants will eventually receive rings. Still, other championship teams have distributed coaches’ rings on opening night, so…

Who are we talking about, exactly? The championship coaching staff included associate head coach Chris Jent, assistants Rick Brunson, Mark Bryant, Darren Erman, Riccardo Fois, Brendan O’Connor, and TJ Saint, along with several player development coaches and advisors (including one of the greatest names in NBA history, the legendary Mo Cheeks!). These were among the people who helped deliver New York’s first NBA championship in 53 years.

To recap: What should have been a celebration of the Knicks’ victory instead exposed tiresome and familiar organizational dysfunction, with coaches handed empty boxes and longtime employees subjected to a misleading phishing exercise. Team owner James Dolan proves once again to be tone-deaf, and this time not by singing at the mic.

A franchise worth billions, a championship decades in the making, and apparently not enough goodwill to go around. How come they win it all and still feel like LOLKnicks?

Read Vardon’s full article here. Go Knicks.

items.title: Game Preview: Knicks at Celtics, October 23, 2026
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
Remember the good old days of just caring about diamond rings, roughly 70 square feet of fabric and the feelings of Ariel Hukporti? Yeah, me neither. It’s what a loss against the Philadelphia 76ers on Banner Night at Madison Square Garden can do to you. It functions as a stark reminder that the new NBA season is upon us and the Knicks somehow have to find a way to let the past be the past and kick some serious you-know-what in the present. On Friday night in Boston, though, it will once again be hard to keep the nostalgia at bay. Even if Mitchell Robinson is not wearing the orange and blue anymore.

The former longest-tenured Knick has moved on to (not so) greener pastures and now starts for one of New York’s biggest rivals a good 200 miles up north. There’s probably no Knicks fan out there who won’t have some weird feeling in their stomach seeing the “Blockness Monster” in a uniform we’ve all been brought up to hate. And if I had to guess, I’d bet that Mr. Robinson puts in quite an effort on the glass tonight. Maybe Mitch even offers a glimpse of an expanded “bag,” as people like to call it these days. He’ll want to show his former team what they’re missing without him and prove to the Land of the Leprechauns that the $48 million they left for him at the end of the free agency rainbow wasn’t fool’s gold.

Celtics still love their three pointers

In Boston’s season opener, Mitch did not make a great impression on the C’s fanbase. Outside of Paul George, though, few players in green and white did. The Celtics lost at Detroit despite leading by 22 four minutes into the third quarter and by 10 with eight minutes left in the fourth. Somehow, someway, that sounds familiar, doesn’t it? And the Boston Celtics haven’t really changed that much from that incredibly entertaining playoff series they played with your beloved Bockers 17 months ago. Their personnel certainly changed, but in terms of their style of play, it’s still bombs away in Beantown.

Boston’s barrage of threes can overwhelm an opponent, just as it did against the Pistons for roughly three quarters on Tuesday, when the Celtics attempted 42 shots from downtown. Their shooting creates a lot of space to operate, puts a lot of stress on the opposing defense and can turn any game in an instant. That cuts both ways, though, because the Celtics really don’t care if they are up by 20 or down by 20. They just keep shooting, and sometimes they shoot themselves in the foot. They certainly did at Detroit, where they let a shell-shocked Pistons team right back into the game with quick shots, nonexistent floor balance and bad transition defense.

The latter part of that contest was especially ugly for Boston, as they allowed 39 points in the final quarter. Their lone remaining superstar, Jayson Tatum, had an awful shooting performance and could not steady his teammates. He missed 17 of his 23 shots and did not provide the much-needed dimension his isolation scoring usually gives Boston from the top of the key. After Jaylen Brown was traded to Philadelphia, the Celtics really do not have that many guys who are comfortable creating their own shot. If Tatum isn’t performing at the All-NBA level he reached before his gruesome Achilles injury, it could become a problem all season long.

First road test for the reigning champions

The one big bright spot for Boston was the play of Paul George, who looked like he wanted to turn back the clock to his old Pacer days. His 38 points were the most ever scored by a Celtic in his debut, and he only needed 21 shots to do it. Not many Bostonians were especially excited to subscribe to the Podcast P experience, but this performance eased at least a few of their worries. Joe Mazzulla’s shot-happy system should suit George quite a bit, and maybe he surprises a lot of people with a solid year.

Besides their two big-name wings, Boston will look to Derrick White and Payton Pritchard to provide most of the scoring. White struggled from the floor in Boston’s first-round playoff loss last season, shooting 32.1 percent, while Pritchard remains one of the elite bench energizers in the entire league. The rest of the Celtics’ rotation includes their three centers, Mitch, Luka Garza and Neemias Queta; a bevy of scrappy younger guys like Hugo Gonzalez, Baylor Scheierman and Jordan Walsh; and elite marksman Sam Hauser. Rookie big Chris Cenac, Mike Conley (yes, he’s still around) and Ron Harper Jr. did not see any action versus Detroit.

Not exactly the scariest bunch on paper, right? Make no mistake, Boston has made a habit of getting consistent results from Mazzulla’s system. They run a professional organization, have a system that more often than not works like a well-oiled machine and have a clear plan for beating their opponent. Tatum is one of the best players in the NBA and surely wants to remind Boston fans that he was the right All-Star wing to build around. So expect a big effort out of him, Mitch and the rest of the Celtics.

For New York, defending the arc and finishing possessions on the glass will be essential, especially with Mitch hunting second chances. Boston’s collapse in Detroit also showed why the Knicks should look to push after misses and take advantage before the Celtics can set their defense. Whatever they throw at New York on Friday won’t surprise our veteran-laden Knickerbockers. But walking into Boston for its home opener and handing the Celtics a second consecutive loss will still be a tall order.

Of course, that’s exactly what we hope to remember from this game. So let’s go Knicks!

Devin Carter will miss the game for the Celtics with mononucleosis. As of this writing, nothing of note for the Knicks.

items.title: The bipolarity of Andre Drummond was on full display on Opening Night
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
One game down, 81 to go. How’s everyone feeling?

You don’t feel well? Chin up; here’s something to cheer you up.

There we are. That’s why we don’t get bent out of shape over individual regular-season games anymore.

There truly wasn’t much to really evaluate from the first game of the season, which acted more as a showcase for the league of Philadelphia’s new starting five and the pizzazz around the Knicks’ banner raising than anything meaningful.

I mean, it was the worst offensive execution of any game this team has played in the 2020s, so unless these guys had the basketball ability sucked out of them like the Monstars at the parade, whatever.

Of all the things that happened on the floor on Opening Night, none intrigued me more than the newest Knick, Andre Drummond. We saw a lot from him due to Karl-Anthony Towns’ early foul trouble.

Early in the game, he looked like the biggest steal of the offseason, posting a double-double with ease and carrying the offense at times.

Late in the game, he was the worst player on the court, throwing away possessions with his poor touch around the rim.

Ladies and gentlemen, from the creators of the “Jameis Winston Experience”, I present to you:

The Andre Drummond Experience.

He wows with some of the best traits you can ask for out of a center. He is one of the best rebounders in NBA history on a rate basis; he sets brick-wall screens, he fills up space. While he’s not a good defender, he’s a lane-clogger on defense.

Then, there’s the flip side. His touch around the rim is diabolically bad. His stocky build makes him an extremely limited defender and a non-existent lob threat. While he’s started working on corner threes, he is still almost exclusively an under-the-rim offensive player.

It’s those two things that separate him from a Mitchell Robinson. While he’s historically more durable than Robinson, he doesn’t give the Knicks the game-breaking defensive ability without putting pressure on the rim. That fast break where Mikal Bridges tried to hit him on a lob, not realizing the 33-year-old can’t really get up there anymore, said everything.

Drummond is good in small doses. It’s why he’s forced to sign these minimum contracts to sit behind All-NBA talents like Joel Embiid and Towns. When you over-expose him, the bad starts to show up a lot more than the good.

We got the full Drummond experience on Tuesday. He had 10 points, 12 rebounds, 3 assists, and 3 stocks in 16 first-half minutes, going 4-for-8 from the field with six offensive rebounds. He was a maniac on the boards, punishing a Sixers team with not much size and not many willing rebounders.

Considering how little they had at their disposal, the Knicks couldn’t have done much better than Drummond in free agency. A lot of their offense over the last few years has been predicated on winning the possession battle. When they miss a three, someone is there to give them a reload. When they miss at the rim, there’s a putback waiting to happen.

When Drummond is on the floor, it’s going to be like Mitch never left offensively… most of the time.

The one glaring problem with having Drummond as your backup center behind a guy like Towns who gets in early foul trouble way too often is that his overexposure really starts to hurt you.

He played a grand total of six minutes in the second half and was a minus-13. He went 1-for-5 from the field, including an airball in the final seconds of the third quarter.

His minutes at the end of the third were especially damaging. The Knicks were leading by five when he entered the game with 3:39 left and trailed by seven when the final horn sounded.

What went wrong? His eyes got too wide offensively.

He and Bridges had a two-man game around the two-minute mark. It looked to be working in the sense that it allowed Mikal to hit him on a bounce pass for what should be an easy floater or rim run, but the Sixers rotated two guys underneath the basket. At this point, Drummond could look up and swing to a wide open OG Anunoby or Deuce McBride.

Instead, he takes a nine-footer that isn’t even close.

Drummond is a very willing passer, especially on offensive rebounds, but plays like these still happen for all seldom-used bigs.

The Knicks were starting to be grilled from deep by a collection of Sixers. Trailing by four in the final minute, Drummond gets the ball in the corner. For a brief second, I thought he would shoot it. It’s not a great shot with 14 on the shot clock, but he’s open and was a passable three-point shooter last season.

Instead, he passed back and the Knicks once again stagnated offensively. He was given a pass in the post with seven on the shot clock, but the defense collapsed and it led to him taking… this shot.

I’m not expecting him to have eyes in the back of his head, but unless it’s a grenade, he should never be attempting whatever that is. All it does is give more energy to your opponent.

After Tyrese Maxey airballed, the Knicks got the ball with 1.5 on the game clock. For some reason, McBride, the former high school quarterback, decided to throw a 50-foot pass to his backup center down the court and airmailed it. This isn’t Drummond’s fault (why was he even out there?), but it involves him.

Jaylen Brown nailed a buzzer-beating three there to cap an 11-0 run to end the third. That sprint by the Sixers wound up costing the Knicks the game.

This stretch doesn’t even include his three baffling missed dunks. He was routinely getting stuffed by Joel Embiid on the interior and couldn’t finish all game, going 5-for-13 on the night.

That is the big crux for Drummond: he is an abysmal finisher for a seven-footer, and he’s progressively getting worse.

Andre Drummond FG% in the restricted area by year, and where he ranked among centers (min. 100 FGA):2025-26: 54.1% (61st/61)2024-25: 59.2% (59th/60)2022-23: 65.5% (56th/64)

Compare that to who he’s replacing in Robinson: the man who has the second-highest field goal percentage in NBA history on a diet of 100% layups and dunks. In 2025-26, Robinson was 25th out of the 61 centers, which doesn’t sound impressive, but his 71.9% is leaps and bounds ahead of Drummond’s dead-last figure.

All told, Knicks fans are going to have a love-hate relationship with Drummond all season long, a man who says the right things and is good natured, but is also the Jameis Winston of the NBA.

An incredibly entertaining, but incredibly inconsistent, ballplayer.

items.title: The King of Cool: P&T’s interview with Walt “Clyde” Frazier
items.author: Andrew Polaniecki
items.content:
If you were to look up the words , , , and in the dictionary, you would find four distinct definitions, each describing a quality that few individuals can truly embody.

Very fashionable, impressive, or appealing in a way that is universally admired.

Possessing a high degree of quality in appearance, design, or behavior.

A natural talent or ability to do things in an original, stylish, and captivating manner.

An individual regarded among the very best to ever perform in a particular field, sport, or profession.

What’s missing alongside each of these definitions in the dictionary is a picture of Walt “Clyde” Frazier. Throughout the storied history of the NBA, countless legends have left their mark on the game, but few, if any, have embodied all four qualities quite like Frazier. From his legendary playing days with the New York Knicks in the 1970s to his continued presence as one of the most recognizable personalities in basketball more than five decades later, Frazier remains in a class of his own, both on and off the court.

A man whose legendary style extends far beyond his flamboyant wardrobe, Frazier helped define an era of New York basketball, captivating fans with his effortless cool, unparalleled court vision, tenacious defense, and undeniable flair.

Widely regarded as one of the greatest players in New York Knicks franchise history, Frazier’s place among basketball royalty is unquestionable. A two-time NBA champion, seven-time NBA All-Star, and member of both the NBA’s 50th and 75th Anniversary Teams, his legacy is as timeless as the city he helped bring to basketball prominence.

Simply put, there has never been another Walt “Clyde” Frazier. And chances are, there never will be.

Let’s start with his style. Clyde’s style was unlike anybody else’s in the NBA during the ‘70s, and to this day, there still hasn’t been a close second. As a young man in his twenties, Frazier became just as recognizable for driving around New York City in his custom Rolls-Royce while sporting a full-length mink coat and fedora as he was for his play on the court. Today, his fashion sense remains as distinctive as ever. Throughout a broadcasting career spanning nearly 40 years, including almost 30 as a television commentator for MSG and the Knicks, his wardrobe has remained unmistakable, from tiger-print suits to custom blazers reminiscent of Joseph’s Technicolor Dreamcoat. There arguably hasn’t been a more fashionable icon in the NBA’s nearly 80-year history.

Frazier was a trendsetter, one of the first NBA players to truly express his personality through his wardrobe, at a time when players were largely known for what they did on the court rather than what they wore off it. His style became a part of his identity, both during his playing days and throughout his broadcasting career, setting him apart from his contemporaries and the generations of NBA stars who followed.

So, just how did Walt Frazier become Clyde?

“Coming to the Mecca. New York City. Fashion, passion,” Frazier explains. “When we played, we wore suits and ties to the game. We were always trying to outdress each other. Our idols were The Temptations, The Four Tops. So we emulated the way these guys performed.”

As Frazier recalls, the influence of Motown played a significant role in shaping his style, much like hip-hop has influenced today’s NBA players.

“Today you see the guys dressed like the rappers… our style was created from Motown. And I took it to another level with the Clyde. One day I bought this wide-brimmed hat and I wore it to the game and everybody go, hey, look at Clyde. And I used to steal the ball on the court.”

But the nickname would eventually become much more than just a reflection of his wardrobe.

“Then I was blessed enough to be the first guy to endorse a sneaker, the Puma Clyde in 1973. So that was the evolution of the mink coat, the Rolls Royce. So it was just my being around New York and observing people watching the Clyde persona personified.”

On the court, Clyde helped lead the Knicks to their first two NBA championships in 1970 and 1973, with the greatest performance of his career coming in Game 7 of the 1970 NBA Finals. With the championship on the line, Frazier delivered one of the most memorable performances in NBA Finals history, scoring 36 points, dishing out a Game 7-record 19 assists, grabbing seven rebounds, and sinking all 12 of his free throws to help secure the Knicks’ first NBA title.

While Clyde’s performance in Game 7 ultimately helped lead the Knicks to their first-ever NBA championship, Clyde and his teammates also received some unexpected motivation from their captain, Willis Reed, who, despite battling a severe leg injury, famously limped onto the court just before tipoff.

“People thought it was premeditated, but we did not know he was coming. So when we came on the court, we were just as flabbergasted as everybody else when we saw him.”

Frazier recalls how Reed’s unexpected appearance immediately changed the team’s confidence.

“By seeing him, it gave us so much confidence. And obviously, he started the game. He made his first two shots. And I thought the Lakers were psyched out from that point, and I would have the game of my life.”

With two NBA championships, seven All-Star appearances, four All-NBA First Team selections, and numerous other accolades to his name, Frazier was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 1987. His No. 10 jersey also hangs in the rafters of Madison Square Garden, making him one of just eight Knicks players to have their numbers retired by the franchise.

But while Frazier’s playing days eventually came to an end, his connection to the Knicks and Madison Square Garden was far from over. In 1987, Clyde began a new chapter with the organization, trading his sneakers for a microphone as he transitioned into broadcasting, where his unmistakable personality and signature style would once again make him a fixture in New York basketball.

Clyde became famous for his iconic on-air rhymes, including “razzlin’ and dazzlin’” and “posting and toasting,” the latter of which inspired the name of our very own website. Frazier explained that his signature rhymes developed naturally as he gained experience in broadcasting and began to understand the nuances of being a color commentator.

“The play-by-play guy does most of the talking on radio. So in order to get into sometimes what I had to say, I had to use rhymes and, you know, that’s how I started doing it.”

With our website’s name paying tribute to one of Clyde’s most recognizable catchphrases, it was only fitting to ask him what he thought about Posting and Toasting.

“Yeah, I read you all the time. I enjoy it, man. It’s very good.”

With the Knicks winning their first championship since 1973, when Clyde hoisted his second trophy, Frazier reflected on the similarities between his championship teams and the current roster.

“It’s an uncanny comparison, man. We personify a team. You can’t mention Frazier without Bradley, without Reed, without Barnett. Same thing with this team. You can’t mention Brunson without Hart, without Bridges, without KAT, without OG. So they personify a team. They’re very unselfish. They like each other. And it’s manifested in the way they play the game.”

And when asked which player from the Knicks’ 2026 championship roster would have fit in best alongside his former teammates, Clyde didn’t hesitate to name the Heart of the City, Josh Hart, pointing to his versatility and physical style of play.

“(Hart) rebounds, he defends, he scores, he plays with reckless abandon. So he would be that type of guy that would fit in our era, which was more physical. You know, we could hand check, push guys around the court. So I think Hart would be perfect for that era.”

As the 2026-27 NBA season tips off on Tuesday, October 20, with the players receiving their championship rings and the Knicks raising their third championship banner to the Madison Square Garden rafters, Clyde is teaming up with Spike Lee and AT&T for a special celebration with Knicks fans. As part of AT&T’s Connectivity Partnership, the two New York icons will travel across Manhattan in a taxi, making surprise appearances and giving fans opportunities to win exclusive NBA merchandise, signed memorabilia, and tickets to opening night.

“I’m teaming up with Spike Lee, and we’re going to be going to different stores, giving out prizes for AT&T, commemorating the next championship season, and rewarding the fans as well. So I can’t believe that. It seems like we’re still in it, man. You know, everybody’s still excited about the team winning and perhaps maybe repeating, you know, running it back, which hasn’t been done in about eight years. We’ll be coming, celebrating this season throughout the season, the Knicks accomplishment. And after 53 years, the Knicks are finally back on top. Fans can walk in peace and celebrate a championship.”

And while the excitement surrounding the Knicks’ championship continues into the new season, perhaps no moment captured the city’s celebration quite like the championship parade itself. As the players celebrated atop their floats and Mitchell Robinson made his way through the streets in his truck, it was only fitting that Clyde, who helped bring New York its first two championships, would lead the celebration through the Canyon of Heroes.

But it wasn’t just Clyde’s presence that made the moment special. It was the car he was riding in.

Frazier led the parade in the very same 1952 Chrysler Imperial Parade Phaeton that carried the Apollo 11 astronauts through the streets of Manhattan following their historic moon landing in 1969. Now that’s cool!

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘We’re the worst team in the NBA’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Isn’t it great to start the season with a loss in the standings…

…and a banner in the rafters?

Here’s what your Knickerbockers and Sixonians said after yesterday’s affair, one of 82 regular-season games. Breathe.

On the Knicks’ championship ring ceremony and the organization’s efforts to organize it:

“I would like to give, and I don’t know who was behind it, but you know, obviously starting with Mr. Dolan and everybody else, you know, did a fantastic job with the ceremony.

“So I would like to acknowledge, you know, everybody else who was behind it. You know, okay, like you said, everybody, you know, you guys did a fantastic job; they weren’t mud like us, so thank you.”

On the Knicks’ performance in their season-opening loss to the 76ers:

“You know, what an ugly game. I want to give the 76ers, Nick Nurse and his team, a lot of credit. A long night for them, but they came out and they tried to do what they needed to do to get a win, so you give them credit first of all. But there were some things that we could have done better. Our transition defense was not good with our starting group in the third quarter. All throughout the game we looked like we were running in mud. Whether it was in the front court or it was in transition, we were not good getting to our spots and putting pressure on Philadelphia the right way… We talked about taking care of the ball. We did a little bit better job. But in a one- or two-possession game when you have 15 turnovers for 22 points, it makes it tough.”

On the Knicks’ slow movement and poor offensive spacing:

“Part of us looking like we were running in mud was our spacing wasn’t great. We were walking everywhere, which hurt our spacing.”

On the Knicks’ transition defense and the 76ers’ fast-break scoring:

“They had nine fast-break points in the first half [in how the Knicks track it]. And then in the second half, they had 19 fast-break points. That’s where the game was won and lost, especially in the third quarter when our starters were out there.”

On how difficult the Knicks’ opening-night performance was to watch:

“I don’t know about you guys, but that was a tough one for me to watch.”

On why a late Jalen Brunson comeback would not have satisfied him even if the Knicks had won the game:

“If Jalen Brunson hits those shots down the stretch and we win, for me personally as their coach, there’s going to be something inside of me that wished it wouldn’t happen. It’s almost like you’re playing with fire and you ended up winning that time without any water or one of them fire blankets to cover the fire.”

On why the Knicks must improve their execution instead of relying on Brunson’s late-game heroics:

“Is (Brunson) capable of making those shots? Yes. But if we played the right way, then it wouldn’t come down to that. But we put ourselves in a hole not doing the little things. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t. And we have to watch the film and regroup and see how we can put a stretch of 48 minutes together.

“I want to win. Don’t get me wrong. Don’t get it twisted. I want to friggin’ win. But not at the expense of us skipping steps. So if he hits those shots down the stretch and we win, as a coach, there’s going to be something inside of me that wouldn’t be happy. Because it’s like you’re playing with fire, and you ended up winning that time without any water.”

On Andre Drummond’s debut:

“I thought that he played with a lot of bounce and energy. We probably ran him a little too long there because it looked like in the second half, not just him but all five of our starters too, ran a little bit out of gas.

“I have to keep getting to know him to see where the minutes may lie for him to be effective for us, but I thought that he was really really, really good on both ends of the floor during the first half.”

On the importance of the little things after the Knicks’ opening-night loss:

“We put ourselves in a hole not doing the other little things and, you know, sometimes it works at the end of the game, sometimes it doesn’t.”

On balancing the Knicks’ championship celebration with their opening-night responsibilities:

“It’s tough because, knock on wood, this could be a once in a lifetime thing. You never know. It’s hard. It’s hard to accomplish something like this.

“You definitely want guys to embrace it and celebrate it with each other because they went through a lot, with the fans, with the rest of the organization, and just with their families. So you don’t want to take that moment away from them. But in the same breath we obviously have a job to do tonight.”

On the Knicks’ slow start not defining their season:

“I keep telling myself that no matter what happens tonight — if we win by five, if we win by 20, if we lose by five, if we lose by 20 — there’s a lot of basketball left. Just because of whatever happens tonight is not going to define us. I would rather them enjoy the moment than me cutting it short or carving into their emotions based on their families and all that stuff being here. Like I said, it’s going to be hard to do, but that’s what we get paid to do so we’ll figure it out one way or another.”

On the atmosphere at Madison Square Garden and the uniqueness of Knicks fans:

“Opening nights are always exciting for everybody and anybody. It’s the start of something new for everybody. It’s fresh. Everybody is energized. You feel the buzz. I don’t care where you are, you feel a buzz. Obviously, here, with our fans, Knicks fans are just different. It’s as simple as that. They’re absolutely friggin’ different. And the buzz has been going on for a while. And you felt it today.

“I had a million texts coming. And usually during the course of the season, I have a couple texts coming before the game. But it was a boatload of them on the way. Couple of calls. … But you can feel it from the correspondence that get, which is different from a regular season game.”

On the Knicks raising a banner to commemorate their 2025 NBA Cup championship:

“I think it’s a recognition of what our journey was like last year. There were obviously a lot of ups and downs. Our guys rallied, found a way to win the NBA Cup and then (the) end-of-season final.”

On the Knicks needing to humble themselves after losing their season opener:

“I think it’s good for us to get knocked down off the mountain, humble ourselves, put our egos in check. I’ve told you guys since day one, whatever happens the first couple of weeks of the season, I’m not sure that’s who we really are.”

On the 76ers’ performance and his own shooting struggles:

“They’re really good and they made things difficult for us. Obvious for me, shots weren’t falling. We can make all the excuses in the world. Like I said, I’m just happy we can move forward now.”

On what failed for the Knicks in Tuesday’s loss:

“Transition defense, yeah. Our offense, I think we were good in spurts. But it’s not good enough.”

On the challenges of defending a championship after receiving so much praise:

“It’s going to be difficult. You have everyone praising us about what we’ve done a couple months ago. It’s just human nature.”

On thanking Knicks fans during the championship banner ceremony:

“Most importantly, I want to say thank you to you guys for not leaving Game 4. We really appreciate it. I mean, this is, as much as we won this, we wouldn’t have won this without you guys, I mean, this is unbelievable. This is really good. A dream come true.

“I know we’re all excited to get this season going. We’re ready to turn the page as a team. But one thing, I would like to say, the joy that this city had this summer we would love to replicate that again. Thank you, guys. Let’s raise this banner.”

On pursuing another NBA championship rather than defending last season’s title:

“Every year, it’s a new year to attack something. When people say we’re defending the title, I mean, that’s one way to look at it. But it’s something we won, we’ve put it in our past, and now we’re just trying to attack another.”

On the Knicks’ mentality after losing their season opener:

“We play basketball for a living. If you can’t get up and get excited to play basketball, no matter who the hell we play, you got to do some soul-searching. It doesn’t matter if we’re defending champs, it doesn’t matter if we have the worst record in the league last year. No matter what we got to make sure we are professionals and do what our job is and at the end of the day, I don’t think anybody picked us to win the championship again.

“So nothing to it. We shouldn’t sit there and think we’re the champions because we’re not. We’re 0-1. We’re the worst team in the NBA as of right now. So we need to play like it.”

On the improved Eastern Conference and the Knicks’ need to dictate how they play:

“Obviously, they played well, and the East got shaken up a little bit. We have to make sure we’re prepared for what every team is going to try and do, and what we want to do. We can’t let them dictate what we want to do. For us, nothing changes. It’s the same ol’ process. We have to make sure we perfect it the best we can.”

On the Knicks failing to match the level of play of last season’s team:

“I just thought that we put ourselves too much in a deficit, and you know we’re not that Knick team yet from last year.”

“To celebrate one last time with the fans, it means a lot. We wanted to give them a better version of ourselves tonight than we did, but it was really special to have that moment here again in New York after 53 years.”

On the Knicks receiving favorable officiating on Tuesday after winning the championship:

“They getting that championship whistle. They win one chip, they get a championship whistle.”

On the 76ers’ defensive rebounding adjustments against the Knicks:

“I thought in the first half we played good first-stop defense, but we gave up some second-chance points. They got some threes off of us not closing with a defensive rebound so. I was really conscious about that [in the second half].”

On the satisfaction of spoiling the Knicks’ championship celebration:

“Yeah, I do (enjoy it). It’s pretty special.”

On the significance of the Knicks’ championship celebration and their 53-year title drought:

“I was a part of that at one point, where we hadn’t won a major championship in Cleveland in over 50 years. The fans will never forget this moment, never forget that championship run. We’re happy that we’re just able to come play on such a historical night, in a historical building, and play the game that we love.”

On the 76ers’ execution in the fourth quarter:

“It’s still going to take some time. It’s one game, but obviously we can learn from the good things that we did, we can learn from the bad things that we did tonight. I thought, in the fourth quarter, we did a good job of executing. We did a good job of pressing the tempo when we got the lead. And when they cut the lead, we made some timely shots.”

On his early chemistry with the 76ers and their defensive performance:

“Obviously, just a little bit over two weeks with the new squad. But yeah, I like the way we played. I think we played exceptionally well, especially defensively.”

On his confrontation with a Knicks fan courtside:

“Ain’t nothing soft about the Midwest, I don’t know what the f–k you talking about. I’m not from the West Coast… I’m from Ohio, baby.”

On defense being the foundation of the 76ers’ opening-night victory:

“Defense is what kept us in it. Defense is what we’ll have to continue to hand our hat on. If we keep a team within 100 [points], we’ll always give ourselves a chance to win. So, it’s non-negotiable. We gotta play defense.”

On spoiling the Knicks’ championship celebration:

“It’s good, what we wanted to do, be a little spoiler. The Knicks’ accomplishment is great, but it’s a new season, new year.”

On whether the 76ers sent a message to the NBA with their win over the reigning champs:

“I don’t think we sent a message. We’re just trying to win as many games as possible, stack days. It’s still early for us. We’re still figuring out a lot of stuff. We still have a lot to learn and grow, but it’s good to learn and grow and win at the same time.”

On the 76ers’ chemistry and potential for improvement:

“I think it was just OK. We got a lot of room for growth, room for improvement. We’re not even at the tip of the iceberg in terms of hitting chemistry … So it’s a good sign that we can win while still being at that early stage.”

On how different the 76ers felt against the Knicks with their new roster:

“I told Tyrese after the game, I was like, ‘We’ve been going against these guys for the last couple of years.’ And, tonight felt a little different.”

On his responsibility to improve the 76ers’ defense:

“I think just we have the talent. I think a lot of it falls on me. I put it on me. If I want to be All-Defense like I used to be, that changes everything for our team. So if I can play that way every single night, which I will, changes everything.”

On Jalen Brunson emerging as one of the faces of the NBA:

“It’s hard not to start with Jalen Brunson. I’ll be down when they hang the banner tonight for the championship. Here’s a guy who was a second-round pick, was picked up as a free agent from Dallas, and nobody talked about him as the next superstar in the league, but look how he’s led that team to a championship.”

On the significance of designing the Knicks’ first championship ring in 53 years:

“This one is easily set apart from the other projects we’ve done because it’s New York City. The city have been waiting for a championship for 53 years. We’re felt the pressure to make sure we delivered something that’s iconic and historic in design, something to be remembered forever.”

On the emotional significance of creating championship rings:

“There’s nothing like a championship ring because it’s more than just a piece of jewelry, it’s a piece of history. I’ve never felt an energy like this before prior to a championship ring delivery. I’ve never felt energy like this before, ever.”

On the design of the removable top of the Knicks’ championship ring:

“We knew that we couldn’t do a feature that’s been done before, so we challenged ourselves to create something new, something different, and something New York would appreciate. New York City is arguably the greatest city on earth. It is the Mecca of basketball, and the arena that symbolizes all of this is Madison Square Garden. When you twist off the top, you see the lower bowl of Madison Square Garden with the court in yellow gold and seats in white gold. The inside of the cap is all hand enameled with the pattern and colors of the ceiling of Madison Square Garden when you’re looking up at the scoreboard.”

On the ring’s miniature Madison Square Garden that rises from its center:

“The unique feature that’s never been done before, the feature that is historic and what New York City deserves, is a feature where you can twist the inner bezel counterclockwise. We have an engineering system that erects a miniature Madison Square Garden from the center of the ring. It literally comes out of the center of the ring and you have an entire Madison Square Garden to scale with the windows, all the architectural features, everything. My jaw dropped when we first finished it.”

On the blue sapphires and the ring’s Madison Square Garden-inspired design:

“There’s the small details that other people might not see. The blue sapphires, the way they’re set behind the Knicks logo on the face of the ring, it mimics the pattern of the ceiling of Madison Square Garden when you’re looking up at the scoreboard.”

On the ring’s concrete texture paying tribute to New York City:

“The background texture of the side of the ring is like a concrete texture, kind of paying homage to the concrete jungle that is New York City. It’s those subtle storylines that you don’t immediately notice, but give the ring a little more depth and meaning.”

On why the Knicks’ championship ring was intentionally extravagant:

“This is an over-the-top ring. It’s supposed to be, because it’s more than just a piece of jewelry. It’s a testament to a moment in time. It’s celebrating a moment in history, something that New York City’s been waiting 53 years for. So, I think that we were able to deliver that.”

On his personal connection to the Knicks and Anthony Mason:

“When we got the call that we got (the business) for this ring, I had tears in my eyes. I can feel the energy of Anthony Mason over my shoulder as he looks down, proud of me, because he started my career by being my first client, and now it’s a full-circle moment where I’m making a Knicks championship ring.”
